title:
Comment of MARY MCCUBBINS in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15423-000
Submission Date: 10/27/2026

documents.name: 151856.txt
documents.text:
MARY MCCUBBINS, KENAI, AK.
Subject: Opposition to DeepGreen's Proposed Cook Inlet Data Center FERC Project No. P-15423-000

Dear FERC,

I am writing to oppose the proposed DeepGreen underwater data center in Cook Inlet, Alaska.
I have serious concerns about what this project could do to the environment, especially since we don't yet know what the long-term effects will be.

One of my biggest concerns is the heat. Computers generate a lot of heat, and this project would put 66 computing pods underwater. The company plans to use the surrounding seawater to cool them, but where does all that heat go? Even if the tides help move the heat around, that doesn't mean it can't affect the areas around the equipment. I want to know how much the water could warm up near the pods as well as the whole of Cook Inlet, especially when the tides are slow. Could it affect salmon, other fish, or the animals that depend on them? I don't think we should assume it's safe without having solid answers first.

I'm also concerned about the endangered Cook Inlet beluga whales and the effects of putting hundreds of turbines and other equipment in their habitat. What about underwater noise, disturbing the seafloor, or metals and other materials leaking into the water over time? These are important questions that deserve real answers before this project moves forward.

I understand that the project is supposed to use tidal power, but I don't think that automatically makes it environmentally friendly. We need to look at the whole picture, including the effects on the water, wildlife, and the surrounding ecosystem.

I believe an independent environmental study should be done before this project moves any further. The public should be able to see the results, and there should be clear rules in place to protect the environment if the project causes problems.

Cook Inlet is too important to take chances with. Once damage is done, we may not be able to undo it. I don't think we should move forward with a project like this until we have a much better understanding of the risks.
I respectfully ask FERC to deny the preliminary permit application.

Thank you for taking the time to consider my concerns.

Sincerely,

Mary McCubbins
Kenai, Alaska
